subskill: same-side interior angles on parallel lines set up as a linear equation, the ACUTE one requested
prompt: Lines l and m are parallel and are cut by a transversal t. Two interior angles that lie on the same side of t, one at l and one at m, measure (4x - 6) degrees and (2x + 18) degrees. What is the measure, in degrees, of the acute angle of the pair?
explanation: Same-side interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary, so (4x - 6) + (2x + 18) = 180, 6x + 12 = 180, x = 28. The two angles are 4(28) - 6 = 106 and 2(28) + 18 = 74, so the acute one is 74. "42" comes from a solver who sets the two angles equal as if they were alternate interior angles, 4x - 6 = 2x + 18, x = 12, and reports 2(12) + 18. "28" is the value of x reported as the angle. "78" comes from a solver who drops the constants when adding, 6x = 180, x = 30, and reports 2(30) + 18.
solve: var x = (180 - 12) / 6; var a = 4 * x - 6, b = 2 * x + 18; return String(Math.min(a, b));

subskill: two isosceles triangles sharing a base angle: a point on the base equidistant from a vertex forces a second pair of equal angles
prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. Point D lies on side BC so that AD = BD, and angle CAD measures 21 degrees. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle ABC?
explanation: Let angle ABC = x. Since AB = AC, angle ACB = x as well. Since AD = BD, triangle ABD is isosceles with angle BAD = angle ABD = x. Then angle BAC = angle BAD + angle CAD = x + 21, and the angle sum of triangle ABC gives x + x + (x + 21) = 180, so 3x = 159 and x = 53. "69" comes from a solver who ignores AD = BD and takes angle BAC to be 2(21) = 42, leaving (180 - 42)/2 for each base angle. "74" is angle BAC, which equals 53 + 21, reported in place of angle ABC. "39" comes from a solver who divides 180 by 3 before removing the 21, 180/3 - 21, instead of subtracting first.

subskill: volume of a prism whose cross-section is a trapezoid joined to a rectangle: a sloping floor that levels off
prompt: A swimming pool is 25 meters long and 10 meters wide. Along its length, the floor is level at a depth of 1.2 meters for the first 8 meters from the shallow end, and then slopes uniformly downward over the remaining 17 meters, reaching a depth of 2.7 meters at the far end. When the pool is full, how many cubic meters of water does it hold?
explanation: Look at the cross-section along the length. The level part is a rectangle 8 by 1.2, area 9.6. The sloping part is a trapezoid with parallel sides 1.2 and 2.7 and width 17, area (1.2 + 2.7)/2 (17) = 33.15. The cross-section is 42.75 square meters, and multiplying by the 10-meter width gives 427.5 cubic meters. "360" comes from a solver who swaps the two section lengths, making the level part 17 meters and the sloping part 8 meters, 10(17(1.2) + 8(1.95)). "420" comes from a solver who assigns the 2.7-meter depth to the 8-meter section and the 1.2-meter depth to the 17-meter section, 10(8(2.7) + 17(1.2)). "331.5" comes from a solver who computes the sloping section correctly but leaves out the level section, 10(17)(1.95).
solve: var flat = 8 * 1.2, slope = (1.2 + 2.7) / 2 * 17; return String(10 * (flat + slope));

subskill: y-intercept of the line perpendicular to a given segment through a stated point
prompt: In the standard (x,y) coordinate plane, line k passes through the points (-2, 7) and (4, 3). Line n is perpendicular to line k and passes through the point (6, -2). What is the y-coordinate of the point where line n crosses the y-axis?
explanation: The slope of line k is (3 - 7)/(4 - (-2)) = -4/6 = -2/3, so the slope of line n is the negative reciprocal, 3/2. Through (6, -2): y = (3/2)(x - 6) - 2, and at x = 0 this gives y = -9 - 2 = -11. "2" comes from a solver who reuses the slope of line k, -2/3, so that y = (-2/3)(0 - 6) - 2 = 2. "-6" comes from a solver who flips only the sign of the slope, 2/3, giving (2/3)(-6) - 2. "7" comes from a solver who takes the reciprocal but not the opposite sign, -3/2, giving (-3/2)(-6) - 2.
solve: var mk = (3 - 7) / (4 - (-2)); var mn = -1 / mk; return String(mn * (0 - 6) + (-2));

subskill: horizontal distance from an angle of depression and a height, using tangent
prompt: From the top of a lighthouse that stands 52 meters above sea level, the angle of depression to a boat is 39 degrees. To the nearest tenth of a meter, how far is the boat from the point at sea level directly below the top of the lighthouse? (Note: sin 39 degrees is about 0.629, cos 39 degrees is about 0.777, and tan 39 degrees is about 0.810.)
explanation: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the boat, so in the right triangle the 52-meter height is opposite the 39-degree angle and the horizontal distance d is adjacent: tan 39 = 52/d, d = 52/0.810, about 64.2 meters. "42.1" comes from a solver who multiplies instead of divides, 52(0.810). "82.7" comes from a solver who uses the sine ratio, 52/0.629, which gives the line-of-sight distance to the boat rather than the horizontal distance. "66.9" comes from a solver who uses the cosine ratio, 52/0.777.

subskill: height of a pole from two guy-wire angles whose anchor points are a known distance apart: two tangent equations in one unknown
prompt: Two guy wires run from the top of a vertical pole to level ground on the same side of the pole. One wire makes an angle of 62 degrees with the ground and the other makes an angle of 48 degrees with the ground, and the two anchor points are 12 meters apart. To the nearest tenth of a meter, how tall is the pole? (Note: sin 48 degrees is about 0.743, tan 48 degrees is about 1.111, sin 62 degrees is about 0.883, and tan 62 degrees is about 1.881.)
explanation: Let h be the height. The steeper wire is anchored h/tan 62 from the pole and the shallower one h/tan 48 from the pole, and the difference between those distances is 12: h/1.111 - h/1.881 = 12. That is h(0.9001 - 0.5316) = 12, so h = 12/0.3685, about 32.6 meters. "22.6" does the same with the 62-degree wire, 12 tan 62. "15.6" comes from a solver who writes the equation with the tangents themselves instead of their reciprocals, h = 12/(tan 62 - tan 48). "56.2" comes from a solver who uses the sine ratio for both wires, as if 12 meters were the difference between the two wire lengths, h = 12/(1/sin 48 - 1/sin 62) with sin 48 about 0.743 and sin 62 about 0.883.

subskill: number of sides of a convex polygon whose interior angles are all equal except one
prompt: In a certain convex polygon, one interior angle measures 90 degrees and every other interior angle measures 150 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
explanation: With n sides, the interior angles sum to 180(n - 2), and here they also sum to 90 + 150(n - 1). Setting 150n - 60 = 180n - 360 gives 30n = 300, so n = 10. Equivalently, the exterior angles are 90 and (n - 1) copies of 30, and 90 + 30(n - 1) = 360 gives n = 10. "12" comes from a solver who ignores the 90-degree angle and treats the polygon as regular with 150-degree angles, 360/30. "9" comes from a solver who uses the exterior-angle sum but counts n copies of 30 alongside the 90, 30n + 90 = 360. "15" comes from a solver who counts n copies of 150 alongside the 90 in the interior sum, 150n + 90 = 180(n - 2).

subskill: inscribed angle from the two arcs the stem does NOT name: the intercepted arc must be found by subtraction from 360
prompt: Points A, B, and C lie on a circle. The arc from A to B that does not contain C measures 96 degrees, and the arc from B to C that does not contain A measures 152 degrees. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle ABC?
explanation: Angle ABC is an inscribed angle whose intercepted arc is the arc from A to C that does not contain B. That arc measures 360 - 96 - 152 = 112 degrees, so angle ABC is half of it, 56 degrees. "76" comes from a solver who halves arc BC, an arc on one side of the vertex, instead of the arc opposite it. "112" is the intercepted arc AC, 360 - 96 - 152, reported without halving. "104" comes from a solver who finds arc AC correctly but then halves arcs AB and AC together, (96 + 112)/2, as if the angle intercepted both.

subskill: arrival clock time from a distance and a speed: a decimal fraction of an hour converted to minutes
prompt: A train leaves a station at 9:47 a.m. and travels 306 kilometers at an average speed of 90 kilometers per hour without stopping. At what time does the train arrive?
explanation: The trip takes 306/90 = 3.4 hours, which is 3 hours and 0.4(60) = 24 minutes. Adding 3 hours 24 minutes to 9:47 a.m. gives 1:11 p.m. "1:27 p.m." comes from a solver who reads the 0.4 of an hour as 40 minutes. "12:51 p.m." comes from a solver who reads 3.4 hours as 3 hours 4 minutes. "1:17 p.m." comes from a solver who rounds 3.4 hours to 3.5 hours and adds 3 hours 30 minutes.
solve: var mins = 9 * 60 + 47 + (306 / 90) * 60; var h = Math.floor(mins / 60), m = Math.round(mins % 60); var h12 = h > 12 ? h - 12 : h; return h12 + ':' + (m < 10 ? '0' + m : m) + ' ' + (h >= 12 ? 'p.m.' : 'a.m.');

var mins = 9 * 60 + 47 + 3 * 60 + 40; var h = Math.floor(mins / 60), m = mins % 60; return (h - 12) + ':' + (m < 10 ? '0' + m : m) + ' p.m.';
var mins = 9 * 60 + 47 + 3 * 60 + 4; var h = Math.floor(mins / 60), m = mins % 60; return h + ':' + (m < 10 ? '0' + m : m) + ' p.m.';
var mins = 9 * 60 + 47 + 3.5 * 60; var h = Math.floor(mins / 60), m = mins % 60; return (h - 12) + ':' + (m < 10 ? '0' + m : m) + ' p.m.';

subskill: recovering an original cost through a markup and a later discount: the two percents multiply and do not add
prompt: A shop prices each item at 40 percent above the shop's cost. During a sale, every item is sold at 30 percent off its shop price. A jacket sells during the sale for $58.80. What was the shop's cost for the jacket?
explanation: Let the cost be c. The shop price is 1.40c and the sale price is 0.70(1.40c) = 0.98c, so 0.98c = 58.80 and c = 60.00. "$53.45" comes from a solver who nets the two percents to a single 10 percent markup and divides by 1.10. "$57.62" comes from a solver who applies the two percents forward to the sale price instead of undoing them, 58.80(1.40)(0.70). "$65.33" comes from a solver who ignores the markup and only undoes the discount, treating the answer as 58.80/0.90 after mistaking the discount for 10 percent net in the other direction.

subskill: mean of the members removed from a group, from the group mean before and after removal
prompt: The mean of 9 test scores is 71. When the two lowest scores are removed, the mean of the remaining 7 scores is 76. What is the mean of the two scores that were removed?
explanation: The 9 scores total 9(71) = 639 and the remaining 7 total 7(76) = 532, so the two removed scores total 639 - 532 = 107 and their mean is 107/2 = 53.5. "66" comes from a solver who assumes each removed score sits 5 points below the original mean, 71 - (76 - 71). "36" comes from a solver who charges the whole 35-point shortfall of the remaining seven, 7(76 - 71), against the original mean as if it fell on a single score. "58.5" comes from a solver who splits that 35-point shortfall between the two removed scores but measures it from the new mean of 76 instead of the old mean.

subskill: overall percent from two subgroup percents weighted by unequal subgroup sizes
prompt: In a survey, 45 percent of the respondents were students and the rest were not. Of the students, 60 percent said they own a bicycle; of the non-students, 20 percent said they own a bicycle. What percent of all the respondents said they own a bicycle?
explanation: Out of every 100 respondents, 45 are students and 55 are not. Bicycle owners number 0.60(45) = 27 among the students and 0.20(55) = 11 among the non-students, 38 in all, so 38 percent. "40%" comes from a solver who averages the two subgroup rates, (60 + 20)/2, ignoring that the subgroups are different sizes. "27%" counts only the student owners and stops. "47%" comes from a solver who adds the students' 27 to the non-students' rate of 20 percent without scaling that rate to the 55 non-students.

subskill: round-trip currency exchange with a percent fee charged each way: four successive multipliers
prompt: A traveler exchanges 500 U.S. dollars for euros at a rate of 0.92 euro per dollar. The exchange office first deducts a 3 percent fee from the dollars and converts the remainder. On returning, the traveler converts all of the euros back to dollars at a rate of 1.08 dollars per euro, and the office again deducts a 3 percent fee from the dollars received. To the nearest cent, how many dollars did the traveler lose over the two exchanges?
explanation: Going out: 500(0.97) = 485 dollars are converted, giving 485(0.92) = 446.20 euros. Coming back: 446.20(1.08) = 481.896 dollars, and after the fee 481.896(0.97) = 467.44 dollars. The loss is 500 - 467.44 = 32.56 dollars. "$30.00" comes from a solver who adds the two 3 percent fees and takes 6 percent of the original 500, ignoring the exchange rates. "$33.20" comes from a solver who treats every change as a percent of the original 500, adding the 6 percent of fees to the 0.64 percent lost to the rates, 500(0.06 + 0.0064). "$99.25" comes from a solver who divides by the return rate of 1.08 instead of multiplying, 500 - 446.20/1.08 (0.97).

subskill: whole boxes rounded UP, and the rounded count is what crosses a discount threshold
prompt: Marco needs 2,000 sheets of card stock. The stock is sold only in boxes of 350 sheets at $18.50 per box, and a 10 percent discount is applied to the whole order when 6 or more boxes are bought in a single order. What is the least amount Marco can pay to get at least 2,000 sheets?
explanation: 2,000/350 is about 5.71, so Marco needs 6 boxes, and an order of 6 boxes qualifies for the discount: 6(18.50)(0.90) = 99.90 dollars. "$111.00" comes from a solver who buys 6 boxes but misses that 6 boxes qualify for the discount, 6(18.50). "$101.00" comes from a solver who reads the 10 percent discount as 10 dollars off, 6(18.50) - 10. "$109.15" comes from a solver who applies the discount only to the box that crosses the threshold, 5(18.50) + 18.50(0.90).
solve: var boxes = Math.ceil(2000 / 350); var cost = boxes * 18.50 * (boxes >= 6 ? 0.90 : 1); return '$' + cost.toFixed(2);

subskill: a fraction of the remainder after a percent is taken from a whole, the remainder itself never stated
prompt: Of the 640 students at a school, 55 percent ride a bus to school. Of the students who do not ride a bus, 3/8 walk and all the others are driven by car. How many of the students are driven by car?
explanation: The students who do not ride a bus number 0.45(640) = 288. Of these, 3/8 walk, which is 108, so the remaining 5/8, or 288 - 108 = 180, are driven. "108" is the number who walk, reported instead of the number driven. "240" comes from a solver who applies the 3/8 to all 640 students instead of to the 288 non-riders. "220" comes from a solver who applies the remaining 5/8 to the 352 bus riders instead of to the 288 non-riders.

subskill: raising a concentration by removing solvent: the solute is fixed while the total shrinks
prompt: A container holds 400 milliliters of a salt solution that is 15 percent salt by volume. How many milliliters of water must evaporate from the container so that the remaining solution is 24 percent salt?
explanation: The salt is fixed at 0.15(400) = 60 milliliters. For that to be 24 percent of the solution, the solution must shrink to 60/0.24 = 250 milliliters, so 400 - 250 = 150 milliliters of water must evaporate. "36" comes from a solver who takes the 9 percentage-point rise as a fraction of the original volume, 0.09(400), as if the salt were being added rather than the water removed. "240" comes from a solver who scales the whole 400 milliliters by the rise over the original percent, (24 - 15)/15 of 400. "127.5" comes from a solver who applies the reduction ratio 1 - 15/24 to the water alone, 340(1 - 15/24), instead of to the whole solution.

subskill: solving a literal linear equation for one variable in terms of another
prompt: If 4(x − 3k) = 7x + 2k, which of the following expresses x in terms of k?
explanation: Distribute on the left: 4x − 12k = 7x + 2k. Collect the x-terms on the left and the k-terms on the right, changing the sign of each term that crosses the equals sign: 4x − 7x = 2k + 12k, so −3x = 14k and x = −14k/3. "10k/3" comes from a solver who moves −12k across without changing its sign, getting −3x = 2k − 12k = −10k. "14k/11" comes from a solver who moves 7x across without changing its sign, getting 4x + 7x = 14k. "-10k/11" comes from a solver who moves both terms across without changing either sign, getting 11x = −10k.
solve: var a = 4, b = 3, c = 7, d = 2; var num = d + a*b, den = a - c; if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; } var p = Math.abs(num), q = den; while (q) { var t = p % q; p = q; q = t; } num /= p; den /= p; return (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + 'k/' + den;

distractor_solve.10k/3: var a = 4, b = 3, c = 7, d = 2; var num = d - a*b, den = a - c; if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; } var p = Math.abs(num), q = den; while (q) { var t = p % q; p = q; q = t; } num /= p; den /= p; return (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + 'k/' + den;
distractor_solve.14k/11: var a = 4, b = 3, c = 7, d = 2; var num = d + a*b, den = a + c; if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; } var p = Math.abs(num), q = den; while (q) { var t = p % q; p = q; q = t; } num /= p; den /= p; return (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + 'k/' + den;
distractor_solve.-10k/11: var a = 4, b = 3, c = 7, d = 2; var num = d - a*b, den = a + c; if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; } var p = Math.abs(num), q = den; while (q) { var t = p % q; p = q; q = t; } num /= p; den /= p; return (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + 'k/' + den;

subskill: solving a radical equation and rejecting the extraneous root introduced by squaring
prompt: What are all real solutions of the equation √(3x + 13) = 5 − x?
explanation: Squaring both sides gives 3x + 13 = 25 − 10x + x², so x² − 13x + 12 = 0 and (x − 1)(x − 12) = 0, giving candidates x = 1 and x = 12. Squaring can introduce solutions that do not satisfy the original equation, so each must be checked. For x = 1: √16 = 4 and 5 − 1 = 4, so it works. For x = 12: √49 = 7 but 5 − 12 = −7, and a principal square root is never negative, so 12 is extraneous. The only solution is 1. "1 and 12" comes from a solver who solves the squared equation and never checks the candidates against the original. "12 only" comes from a solver who checks against x − 5 instead of 5 − x, which accepts 12 (7 = 7) and rejects 1 (4 ≠ −4). "no real solution" comes from a solver who squares 5 − x as 25 + x², dropping the middle term, and gets x² − 3x + 12 = 0, whose discriminant is negative.
solve: var A = 1, B = -13, C = 12; var D = B*B - 4*A*C; var roots = []; if (D >= 0) { var r1 = (-B - Math.sqrt(D)) / (2*A), r2 = (-B + Math.sqrt(D)) / (2*A); roots = r1 === r2 ? [r1] : [r1, r2]; } var ok = roots.filter(function (r) { var rhs = 5 - r; return rhs >= 0 && Math.abs(Math.sqrt(3*r + 13) - rhs) < 1e-9; }); if (ok.length === 0) return 'no real solution'; if (ok.length === 1) return String(ok[0]) + ' only'; return ok.join(' and ');

subskill: a single coefficient in the product of a quadratic and a quadratic, collected from three partial products
prompt: When (2x² − 3x + 1)(x² + 5x − 4) is expanded and like terms are combined, what is the coefficient of x²?
explanation: An x² term in the product arises from three pairings: 2x² times −4 gives −8x², −3x times 5x gives −15x², and 1 times x² gives x². Adding them, −8 − 15 + 1 = −22. "-6" comes from a solver who takes the product of 2x² and −4 as +8x², getting 8 − 15 + 1. "7" comes from a solver who collects the x³ terms instead: 2x² times 5x gives 10x³ and −3x times x² gives −3x³, so 10 − 3 = 7. "17" comes from a solver who collects the x terms instead: −3x times −4 gives 12x and 1 times 5x gives 5x, so 12 + 5 = 17.
solve: var P = [1, -3, 2], Q = [-4, 5, 1]; var R = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]; for (var i = 0; i < P.length; i++) for (var j = 0; j < Q.length; j++) R[i + j] += P[i] * Q[j]; return String(R[2]);

distractor_solve.7: var P = [1, -3, 2], Q = [-4, 5, 1]; var R = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]; for (var i = 0; i < P.length; i++) for (var j = 0; j < Q.length; j++) R[i + j] += P[i] * Q[j]; return String(R[3]);

distractor_solve.-6: var P = [1, -3, 2], Q = [-4, 5, 1]; var R = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]; for (var i = 0; i < P.length; i++) for (var j = 0; j < Q.length; j++) { var v = P[i] * Q[j]; if (i === 2 && j === 0) v = Math.abs(v); R[i + j] += v; } return String(R[2]);

subskill: the value of a coefficient that makes a system of two linear equations have no solution
prompt: For what value of k does the system 2x − 3y = 11 and kx + 12y = 5 have no solution?
explanation: A system of two linear equations has no solution when the lines are parallel and distinct, which happens when the coefficients of x and y are proportional but the constants are not. Here 12 is −4 times −3, so k must be −4 times 2, giving k = −8. Then the second equation is −8x + 12y = 5, while −4 times the first is −8x + 12y = −44, so the lines are indeed distinct. Equivalently, the slopes 2/3 and −k/12 must be equal, so −k/12 = 2/3 and k = −8. "8" comes from a solver who drops the sign, scaling by 4 instead of −4 because 12 is 4 times 3. "-1/2" comes from a solver who inverts the proportion, writing k/12 = −3/2 and solving for k as though 2 sat under 12, which gives k = 2(−3)/12. "1/2" comes from a solver who both inverts the proportion and drops the sign, computing 2(3)/12.
solve: var a1 = 2, b1 = -3, a2 = 12; var num = a1 * a2, den = b1; if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; } var p = Math.abs(num), q = den; while (q) { var t = p % q; p = q; q = t; } num /= p; den /= p; return den === 1 ? String(num) : (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + '/' + den;

String(num) : (num < 0 ? '-' : '') + Math.abs(num) + '/' + den;
